claim: Human fibroblasts from postnatal to near centenarian donors can be efficiently converted into neurons using microRNA-based cellular reprogramming.
source: Here, we show that using a recently demonstrated microRNA-based cellular reprogramming approach, human fibroblasts from postnatal to near centenarian donors can be efficiently converted into neurons that maintain multiple age-associated signatures.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating conversion efficiency across age ranges.

claim: Neurons converted from fibroblasts using microRNA-based reprogramming maintain multiple age-associated signatures.
source: Here, we show that using a recently demonstrated microRNA-based cellular reprogramming approach, human fibroblasts from postnatal to near centenarian donors can be efficiently converted into neurons that maintain multiple age-associated signatures.
evidence: The abstract states this as a main finding, supported by multiple types of data including epigenetic clock, transcriptome, microRNA profiles, and cellular assays presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The epigenetic ages of fibroblasts are highly correlated with corresponding age estimates of reprogrammed neurons.
source: Application of an epigenetic biomarker of aging (referred to as epigenetic clock) to DNA methylation data revealed that the epigenetic ages of fibroblasts were highly correlated with corresponding age estimates of reprogrammed neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data analyzed using the epigenetic clock method, showing correlation of 0.91 (p=2.5e-06) as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transcriptome and microRNA profiles reveal genes differentially expressed between young and old neurons.
source: Transcriptome and microRNA profiles reveal genes differentially expressed between young and old neurons.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data presented in Figure 3, showing differential gene and microRNA expression patterns between young and old reprogrammed neurons.

claim: Oxidative stress, DNA damage and telomere length exhibit the retention of age-associated cellular properties in converted neurons from corresponding fibroblasts.
source: Further analyses of oxidative stress, DNA damage and telomere length exhibit the retention of age-associated cellular properties in converted neurons from corresponding fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from MitoSOX assays (Figure 4A), Comet assays (Figure 4B), and telomere length analyses (Figure 4C).

claim: Aging is a major risk factor in many forms of late-onset neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Aging is a major risk factor in many forms of late-onset neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the relationship between aging and neurodegeneration.

claim: Age-related neurodegeneration may be caused in part by cellular aging processes that result in accumulation of damaged DNA and proteins in neurons.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that in addition to genetic susceptibility, age-related neurodegeneration may be caused in part by cellular aging processes that result in accumulation of damaged DNA and proteins in neurons (Mattson and Magnus, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mattson and Magnus, 2006.

claim: Studying age-related cellular processes in human neurons from elderly individuals remains a difficult task due to inaccessibility.
source: However, because of the inaccessibility to neurons from elderly individuals, studying these age-related cellular processes in human neurons remains a difficult task.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the practical challenges of obtaining neurons from living elderly individuals.

claim: Induction of pluripotency in adult fibroblasts reverts cellular age to an embryonic stage.
source: Importantly, this induction of pluripotency in adult fibroblasts reverts cellular age to an embryonic stage (Lapasset et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2012) which remains even after differentiation into neurons (Patterson et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lapasset et al., 2011 and Patterson et al., 2012.

claim: The age reversion in iPSCs remains even after differentiation into neurons.
source: Importantly, this induction of pluripotency in adult fibroblasts reverts cellular age to an embryonic stage (Lapasset et al., 2011; Patterson et al., 2012) which remains even after differentiation into neurons (Patterson et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Patterson et al., 2012 and Miller et al., 2013.

claim: iPSC-derived cells have been reported to be unsuitable in recapitulating phenotypes selectively observed in aged cells.
source: While this is useful for modeling early developmental phenotypes (Lafaille et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2009), iPSC-derived cells have been reported to be unsuitable in recapitulating phenotypes selectively observed in aged cells (Mattson and Magnus, 2006; Vera and Studer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mattson and Magnus, 2006 and Vera and Studer, 2015.

claim: Overexpressing progerin can force the detection of age-related pathophysiology of neurodegenerative disease in iPSC-derived cells.
source: Recently, experimental manipulations to accelerate aging in iPSC-derived cells have been explored, for instance, by overexpressing progerin, a mutant form of lamin A observed in progeria syndrome, to force the detection of age-related pathophysiology of neurodegenerative disease (Arbab et al., 2014; Cornacchia and Studer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arbab et al., 2014 and Cornacchia and Studer, 2015.

claim: Neuronal microRNAs miR-9/9* and miR-124 can directly convert human fibroblasts to specific mature neuronal subtypes.
source: Alternatively, we previously described a reprogramming paradigm using neuronal microRNAs (miRNAs), miR-9/9* and miR-124 (miR-9/9*-124), that exert reprogramming activities to directly convert human fibroblasts to specific mature neuronal subtypes (Richner et al., 2015; Victor et al., 2014; Yoo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Richner et al., 2015; Victor et al., 2014; Yoo et al., 2011).

claim: MiRNA-mediated directly reprogrammed neurons would retain the age signature of the original donor because neuronal conversion bypasses pluripotent/multipotent stem cell stages.
source: Because this neuronal conversion is direct and bypasses pluripotent/multipotent stem cell stages, we reasoned that miR-mediated directly reprogrammed neurons would retain the age signature of the original donor.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of direct conversion avoiding pluripotency, which is known to reset age.

claim: The epigenetic clock method is a highly accurate biomarker of age based on DNA methylation.
source: To assess the cellular age, we used the epigenetic clock method, which is a highly accurate biomarker of age based on DNA methylation (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013, which describes the epigenetic clock method.

claim: Fibroblast samples from donors ranging from 3 days to 96 years of age were collected and expanded to match population doubling level.
source: Fibroblast samples from donors ranging from 3 days to 96 years of age were collected and expanded to match population doubling level (PDL) to eliminate any confounding variability introduced by sequential passaging (Campisi and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2007; Pazolli and Stewart, 2008), then subsequently transduced with miR-9/9*-124 with CTIP2, DLX1/2, and MYT1L (CDM) following our established protocol (Richner et al., 2015; Victor et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology, with citations supporting the rationale for PDL matching and references to the established protocol.

claim: MAP2 and TUBB3-positive reprogrammed neurons exhibiting extensive neurite outgrowth represented approximately 70-80% of the cell population.
source: MAP2 and TUBB3-positive reprogrammed neurons exhibiting extensive neurite outgrowth represented approximately 70–80% of the cell population (Figure 1D), demonstrating the consistency of reprogramming efficiency in all fibroblast samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reprogrammed neurons from young and old fibroblasts exhibited fast inward currents and action potentials in monocultures without necessitating coculturing with glial cells or primary neurons.
source: Neurons reprogrammed from young and old fibroblasts exhibited fast inward currents and action potentials in monocultures without necessitating coculturing with glial cells or primary neurons (n = 11) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1E from 11 recorded neurons.

claim: Consistent upregulation of neuronal genes, including MAP2, NCAM, and voltage-gated sodium channels, and downregulation of fibroblast-associated genes were observed in reprogrammed neurons from both young and old cells.
source: In addition, the consistent upregulation of neuronal genes, including MAP2, NCAM, and voltage-gated sodium channels, and downregulation of fibroblast-associated genes were observed in reprogrammed neurons from both young and old cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The actual chronological donor age was highly correlated with the estimated DNAm age of fibroblasts (correlation = 0.75).
source: The actual chronological donor age was highly correlated with the estimated DNAm age of fibroblasts (correlation = 0.75) (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis data shown in Figure 2B with statistical correlation value.

claim: The actual chronological donor age was highly correlated with the estimated DNAm age of reprogrammed neurons (correlation = 0.82).
source: The actual chronological donor age was highly correlated with the estimated DNAm age of fibroblasts (correlation = 0.75) (Figure 2B) and of reprogrammed neurons (correlation = 0.82) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis data shown in Figure 2B with statistical correlation value.

claim: The DNAm age of each reprogrammed neuron was highly correlated with the DNAm age of the corresponding fibroblast (correlation = 0.91).
source: Importantly, when the DNAm age of each reprogrammed neuron was compared to the DNAm age of the corresponding fibroblast, there was a near-perfect correlation (correlation = 0.91), which suggests that the epigenetic clock is unperturbed during miRNA-based neuronal reprogramming (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis data shown in Figure 2C with statistical correlation value.

claim: The epigenetic clock is unperturbed during miRNA-based neuronal reprogramming.
source: Importantly, when the DNAm age of each reprogrammed neuron was compared to the DNAm age of the corresponding fibroblast, there was a near-perfect correlation (correlation = 0.91), which suggests that the epigenetic clock is unperturbed during miRNA-based neuronal reprogramming (Figure 2C) and supports the notion of age maintenance during direct neuronal conversion.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation (0.91) between fibroblast and reprogrammed neuron DNAm ages.

claim: iPSC generation resets the epigenetic clock to an embryonic state since iPSCs have a DNAm age that is negative or close to zero.
source: By contrast, it is known that iPSC generation resets the epigenetic clock to an embryonic state since iPSCs have a DNAm age that is negative or close to zero (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: Principal component analysis of transcriptome revealed cell type-specific clustering of reprogrammed neurons versus fibroblasts.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of transcriptome revealed cell type-specific clustering of reprogrammed neurons versus fibroblasts, while age-associated segregation is observed in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Age-associated segregation is observed in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons in transcriptome analysis.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of transcriptome revealed cell type-specific clustering of reprogrammed neurons versus fibroblasts, while age-associated segregation is observed in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A cohort of upregulated and downregulated genes with aging was commonly observed in both fibroblasts and converted neurons.
source: A cohort of upregulated and downregulated genes with aging was commonly observed in both fibroblasts and converted neurons (Figure 3B), consistent with a previous report (Mertens et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with a cited previous report.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes with age in reprogrammed neurons is enriched for terms associated with age-related biological processes including vesicle-mediated transport, nervous system development, NF-kappaB transcription factor activity, regulation of apoptosis and inflammatory response.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed genes with age in reprogrammed neurons is enriched for terms associated with age-related biological processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), including vesicle-mediated transport (Wilmot et al., 2008), nervous system development (Lu et al., 2004) NF-kappaB transcription factor activity (Tilstra et al., 2011), regulation of apoptosis and inflammatory response (de Magalhães et al., 2009), and for genes previously identified to be associated with age in the human brain (Lu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to relevant literature.

claim: MicroRNA profiling revealed distinct sample segregation both with age (young versus old) and cell type (fibroblasts versus reprogrammed neurons).
source: MicroRNA profiling similarly revealed distinct sample segregation both with age (young versus old) and cell type (fibroblasts versus reprogrammed neurons) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microRNA profiling data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fourteen microRNAs were commonly regulated with age in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons, including miR-10a, miR-497, and miR-195, whose expression increased with age.
source: Interestingly, we detected fourteen microRNAs commonly regulated with age in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons, including miR-10a, miR-497, and miR-195, whose expression increased with age (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by microRNA profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: MicroRNAs have been implicated as global regulators of aging-associated cellular processes through repression of existing target transcripts.
source: Because microRNAs have been implicated as global regulators of aging-associated cellular processes (Liu et al., 2012; Harries, 2014) through repression of existing target transcripts (He and Hannon, 2004; Pasquinelli, 2012; Lewis et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: GO analysis of predicted targets amongst age-downregulated transcripts in reprogrammed neurons for miR-10a-5p and miR-497-5p revealed terms associated with age such as metabolism and cellular death and survival.
source: Indeed, GO analysis of predicted targets amongst age-downregulated transcripts in reprogrammed neurons (Figure 3B) for miR-10a-5p and miR-497-5p revealed terms associated with age such as metabolism and cellular death and survival (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: miR-10a and miR-497 have been previously implicated in aging-associated cellular processes including inflammation, senescence, metabolism and telomerase activity.
source: While the exact role of these microRNAs in aging is unknown, miR-10a and miR-497 have been previously implicated in aging-associated cellular processes including inflammation, senescence, metabolism and telomerase activity (Kondo et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kondo et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2012; Fang et al., 2010.

claim: The increased expression of miR-10a, miR-497 and miR-195 detected in reprogrammed neurons was concordantly upregulated in human striatum and cortex samples from old individuals in comparison to young individuals.
source: Importantly, the increased expression of miR-10a, miR-497 and miR-195 detected in reprogrammed neurons was also validated by qPCR to be concordantly upregulated in human striatum and cortex samples from old individuals in comparison to young individuals (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR validation data shown in Figure 3E comparing reprogrammed neurons to human brain tissue samples.

claim: Oxidative stress has been reported to increase with age, in part due to the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Oxidative stress has been reported to increase with age, in part due to the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Keating, 2008; Prigione et al., 2010; Suhr et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Old reprogrammed neurons have increased ROS levels compared to young reprogrammed neurons.
source: FACS analysis of ROS levels using fluorescent marker MitoSOX (Miller et al., 2013) revealed that old reprogrammed neurons have increased ROS levels compared to young reprogrammed neurons, mirroring the observed age-associated differences of ROS levels in fibroblasts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Old reprogrammed neurons have longer comet tail lengths, reflecting more extensive DNA damage accumulation compared to young cells.
source: Old reprogrammed neurons were found to have longer comet tail lengths, an age-associated property also observed in fibroblasts, that reflects more extensive DNA damage accumulation compared to young cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Comet Assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neuronal conversion maintained the length of telomeres from starting fibroblast which is virtually unchanged.
source: Additionally, neuronal conversion maintained the length of telomeres from starting fibroblast which is virtually unchanged (Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by telomere length analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: iPSC reprogramming results in progressive increase in telomere length, reaching a plateau of around 12-14 kilobases after a few cellular passages.
source: Additionally, neuronal conversion maintained the length of telomeres from starting fibroblast which is virtually unchanged (Figure 4C), in contrast to the progressive increase in length commonly observed with iPSC reprogramming, where telomeres reach a plateau of around 12–14 kilobases after a few cellular passages (Agarwal et al., 2010; Batista et al., 2011; Marion et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2010; Batista et al., 2011; Marion et al., 2009.

claim: Directly converted neurons may serve as an alternative model of neuronal aging to iPSC-derived neurons.
source: Because aging is a complex process affecting many hallmarks of a cell (López-Otín et al., 2013), our assessment of a broad spectrum of age-related markers suggests that directly converted neurons may serve as an alternative model of neuronal aging to iPSC-derived neurons, whose erasure of multiple aging-associated signatures precludes it from adequately modeling, especially, late-onset diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing maintenance of multiple age signatures in directly converted neurons, contrasted with the known age erasure in iPSC-derived neurons.

claim: iPSC-derived neurons' erasure of multiple aging-associated signatures precludes them from adequately modeling late-onset diseases.
source: Because aging is a complex process affecting many hallmarks of a cell (López-Otín et al., 2013), our assessment of a broad spectrum of age-related markers suggests that directly converted neurons may serve as an alternative model of neuronal aging to iPSC-derived neurons, whose erasure of multiple aging-associated signatures precludes it from adequately modeling, especially, late-onset diseases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about iPSC age erasure and logical inference about its implications for disease modeling.

claim: Older fibroblasts have lower replicative potential in culture.
source: While miR-9/9*-124-based reprogramming can directly convert fibroblasts with similar efficiency to neurons, we note that the older fibroblasts have lower replicative potential in a culture.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work, representing established knowledge about cellular senescence.

claim: Lower replicative potential of older fibroblasts does not impede the conversion efficiency of old fibroblasts.
source: While miR-9/9*-124-based reprogramming can directly convert fibroblasts with similar efficiency to neurons, we note that the older fibroblasts have lower replicative potential in a culture. However, this does not impede in the conversion efficiency of old fibroblasts.
evidence: This is based on the observation that conversion efficiency remains consistent across ages despite lower replicative potential.

claim: The epigenetic clock analyzes the methylation status of 353 specific CpG loci.
source: The epigenetic clock, which analyzes the methylation status of 353 specific CpG loci, has been shown to be a highly accurate age estimator that applies to all human organs, tissues, and cell types (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the epigenetic clock method, supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: The epigenetic clock has been shown to be a highly accurate age estimator that applies to all human organs, tissues, and cell types.
source: The epigenetic clock, which analyzes the methylation status of 353 specific CpG loci, has been shown to be a highly accurate age estimator that applies to all human organs, tissues, and cell types (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horvath, 2013.

claim: DNA methylation levels of neurons converted from 16 fibroblast samples aged three days to 96 years alongside 37 fibroblast samples aged three days to 94 years were analyzed.
source: We analyzed DNA methylation levels of neurons converted from 16 fibroblast samples aged three days to 96 years alongside 37 fibroblast samples aged three days to 94 years (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample set used for DNA methylation analysis.

claim: Age-associated transcriptomic changes are maintained in neurons directly converted by transcription factors.
source: Given the broad variability in gene expression with age in multiple cell types (Berchtold et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2004; Fraser et al., 2005; Glass et al., 2013) and a recent demonstration of maintenance of age-associated transcriptomic changes in neurons directly converted by transcription factors (Mertens et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mertens et al., 2015.

claim: Reprogrammed cells were stained for neuronal markers MAP2, TUBB3, NeuN and MSN markers DARPP32 and GABA.
source: Reprogrammed cells were then stained for neuronal markers, MAP2, TUBB3, NeuN and MSN markers, DARPP32 and GABA (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology for characterizing reprogrammed neurons.

claim: All reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts recorded (n = 11) fired action potentials in response to current injections.
source: All reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts recorded (n = 11) fired APs in response to current injections (top).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Upregulation of neuronal genes and downregulation of fibroblast-associated genes occur in reprogrammed neurons from both young and old fibroblasts.
source: Heatmap of representative DEGs: upregulation of neuronal genes (top) and downregulation of fibroblast associated genes (bottom) in reprogrammed neurons from both young and old fibroblasts (right) when compared to corresponding fibroblasts (left).
evidence: This claim is supported by heatmap data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The epigenetic age is predictive of all-cause mortality even after adjusting for a variety of known risk factors.
source: The epigenetic clock has been shown to capture aspects of biological age: the epigenetic age is predictive of all-cause mortality even after adjusting for a variety of known risk factors (Marioni et al., 2015; Christiansen et al., 2016; Horvath et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marioni et al., 2015; Christiansen et al., 2016; Horvath et al., 2015a.

claim: The utility of the epigenetic clock method has been demonstrated in applications surrounding cognitive function, obesity, Down syndrome, HIV infection, and Parkinson's disease.
source: The utility of the epigenetic clock method has been demonstrated in applications surrounding cognitive function (Levine et al., 2015), obesity (Horvath et al., 2014), Down syndrome (Horvath et al., 2015b), HIV infection (Horvath and Levine, 2015), and Parkinson's disease (Horvath and Ritz, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies applying the epigenetic clock to various conditions.

claim: Fibroblasts were expanded to a population doubling level (PDL) of approximately 19-21.
source: Fibroblast cell lines were expanded to a population doubling level (PDL) of ~19–21.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology for cell culture.

claim: Reprogrammed neurons were analyzed after 30 days of ectopic expression of miR-9/9*-124-CDM.
source: Reprogrammed neurons were harvested after 30 days of ectopic expression of miR-9/9*-124-CDM.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline for neuronal conversion.

claim: ROS levels in old reprogrammed neurons show a significant difference compared to young reprogrammed neurons (p-value=0.019).
source: Quantification of percent of cells positive for MitoSOX reveals a significant difference in fibroblasts with age in addition to reprogrammed neurons with age. ***p-value=0.0008; *p-value=0.019.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4A with statistical significance values.

claim: Comet tail lengths in old reprogrammed neurons are significantly longer than in young reprogrammed neurons (p-value=0.004).
source: Quantification of tail lengths in fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons with age *p-value=0.013, **p-value=0.004.
evidence: This claim is supported by Comet Assay quantification data shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance values.

claim: Telomere length analyses were performed on reprogrammed neurons from one year old, 56 year old, and 86 year old donors.
source: Telomere length analyses of reprogrammed neurons are maintained from corresponding starting fibroblasts from one year old, 56 year old, and 86 year old donors.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for telomere length analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: miR-9/9*-124 with CTIP2, DLX1/2, and MYT1L can robustly generate a highly enriched population of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs) from fibroblasts.
source: We therefore elected to test our recently developed conversion approach that utilizes miR-9/9*-124 and transcription factors to robustly generate a highly enriched population of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs) from the fibroblasts of donors of varying ages (Richner et al., 2015; Victor et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Richner et al., 2015 and Victor et al., 2014, and demonstrated by data in Figure 1.

claim: Fibroblast samples were expanded to match population doubling level to eliminate any confounding variability introduced by sequential passaging.
source: Fibroblast samples from donors ranging from 3 days to 96 years of age were collected and expanded to match population doubling level (PDL) to eliminate any confounding variability introduced by sequential passaging (Campisi and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2007; Pazolli and Stewart, 2008)
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations explaining the rationale for PDL matching.

claim: The Comet Assay is a single-cell gel electrophoresis technique that assesses DNA damage accumulation.
source: Moreover, reprogrammed neurons were analyzed by Comet Assay, a single-cell gel electrophoresis technique that assesses DNA damage accumulation (Singh et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a description of the Comet Assay method, supported by citation to Singh et al., 1990.

claim: Four microRNAs (miR-10a, miR-497, miR-10b, and miR-195) are upregulated with age in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons.
source: MicroRNAs that are differentially regulated with age in both fibroblasts (red) and reprogrammed neurons (blue). Four microRNAs, miR-10a, miR-497, miR-10b, and miR-195, are upregulated with age, while 10 microRNAs are shown to be downregulated with age, p<0.05.
evidence: This claim is supported by microRNA profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ten microRNAs are downregulated with age in both fibroblasts and reprogrammed neurons.
source: MicroRNAs that are differentially regulated with age in both fibroblasts (red) and reprogrammed neurons (blue). Four microRNAs, miR-10a, miR-497, miR-10b, and miR-195, are upregulated with age, while 10 microRNAs are shown to be downregulated with age, p<0.05.
evidence: This claim is supported by microRNA profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GO analysis of age-downregulated transcripts in reprogrammed neurons shows enrichment for metabolic process, intracellular transport, vesicle-mediated transport, nervous system development, and regulation of apoptosis.
source: GO analysis of age-downregulated transcripts (top) and upregulated transcipts (bottom) in reprogrammed neurons, log fc > 1, FDR < 0.01 using BiNGO from Cytoscape version 3.3.0. (FDR 0.05). GO terms related to aging-associated processes are represented here.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GO analysis of age-upregulated transcripts in reprogrammed neurons shows enrichment for defense response, signaling, inflammatory response, and cytolysis.
source: GO analysis of age-downregulated transcripts (top) and upregulated transcipts (bottom) in reprogrammed neurons, log fc > 1, FDR < 0.01 using BiNGO from Cytoscape version 3.3.0. (FDR 0.05). GO terms related to aging-associated processes are represented here.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Predicted targets of miR-10a-5p among age-downregulated transcripts are enriched for GO terms including gene expression, cell death and survival, and cellular development.
source: GO analysis of list of age-downregulated transcripts predicted to be targeted by upregulated microRNAs, miR-10a-5p (top) and miR-497-5p (bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Predicted targets of miR-497-5p among age-downregulated transcripts are enriched for GO terms including cell death and survival, cellular assembly and organization, and cell cycle.
source: GO analysis of list of age-downregulated transcripts predicted to be targeted by upregulated microRNAs, miR-10a-5p (top) and miR-497-5p (bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Validation of miRNA expression was conducted in reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts aged 89, 90, 91, 92, 92, 94 compared to reprogrammed neurons from young fibroblasts aged three days, five months, one, two, 12 years of age.
source: QPCR validation of miRNA expression was conducted in reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts aged 89, 90, 91, 92, 92, 94 compared to reprogrammed neurons from young fibroblasts aged three days, five months, one, two, 12 years of age.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for qPCR validation.

claim: QPCR experiments were conducted with human striatum and human cortex slices acquired from young individuals aged 9, 11, and 19 years compared to those from older individuals aged 83, 85, and 87 years.
source: QPCR experiments were conducted with human striatum and human cortex slices acquired from young individuals aged 9, 11, and 19 years compared to those from older individuals aged 83, 85, and 87 years.
evidence: This is a description of the human brain tissue samples used for qPCR validation.

claim: Young samples for MitoSOX analysis included reprogrammed neurons from fibroblasts aged three days, five month, one year and two years.
source: Young samples included reprogrammed neurons from fibroblasts aged three days, five month, one year and two years, while old samples were from donors aged 86, 90, 91, 92A, and 92B years.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for MitoSOX analysis.

claim: Old samples for MitoSOX analysis were from donors aged 86, 90, 91, 92A, and 92B years.
source: Young samples included reprogrammed neurons from fibroblasts aged three days, five month, one year and two years, while old samples were from donors aged 86, 90, 91, 92A, and 92B years.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for MitoSOX analysis.

claim: Comet assay analysis compared reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts aged 91, 92A and 92B to reprogrammed neurons from young fibroblasts aged three days, five months, and one year old.
source: Tails lengths were measured by drawing a region of interest and p-values were calculated with student t-test for reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts aged 91, 92A and 92B compared to reprogrammed neurons from young fibroblasts aged three days, five months, and one year old
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for Comet assay analysis.

claim: Analyzed fibroblasts for Comet assay were aged five months, one year, 12, 72, 86, and 92 years of age.
source: Tails lengths were measured by drawing a region of interest and p-values were calculated with student t-test for reprogrammed neurons from old fibroblasts aged 91, 92A and 92B compared to reprogrammed neurons from young fibroblasts aged three days, five months, and one year old, while analyzed fibroblasts were aged five months, one year, 12, 72, 86, and 92 years of age.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for Comet assay analysis.

claim: Genomic DNA was collected from reprogrammed neurons from fibroblasts from one year, 56, and 86 year old donors and the corresponding fibroblasts for telomere analysis.
source: Genomic DNA was collected from reprogrammed neurons from fibroblasts from one year, 56, and 86 year old donors and the corresponding fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental samples used for telomere length analysis.

claim: Transduced fibroblasts were maintained in fibroblast media for two days with doxycycline prior to selection with Puromycin and Blasticidin at day three.
source: Briefly, transduced fibroblasts were maintained in fibroblast media for two days with doxycycline prior to selection with Puromycin (3 μg/ml) and Blasticidin (5 μg/ml) at day three
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol for neuronal reprogramming.

claim: Cells were maintained in Neuronal Media supplemented with valproic acid, dibutyryl cAMP, BDNF, NT-3, and RA for 30-35 days before analysis.
source: Cells were subsequently maintained in Neuronal Media (ScienCell, Carlsbad, CA) supplemented with valproic acid (1 mM), dibutyryl cAMP (200 μM), BDNF (10 ng/ml), NT-3 (10 ng/ml), and RA (1 μM) for 30–35 days before analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol for neuronal reprogramming.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed at four weeks after transduction with miR-9/9*-124-CDM.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed at four weeks after transduction with miR-9/9*-124-CDM.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline for electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Membrane potentials were typically kept at −60 mV to −70 mV during electrophysiology recordings.
source: Membrane potentials were typically kept at −60 mV to −70 mV.
